To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the accumulation of viral transcripts and DNA during acute ganglioneural infection is similar in wild-type- or thymidine kinase-deficient HSV-1-infected ganglia, but that the accumulation of DNA is greater in wild-type-infested ganglia than in mutant-infected ones.

during establishment of latent infection in mouse trigemial ganglia, viral DNA and latency-associated transcripts accumulate to levels comparable to those in wild-type-inflicted ganglia during acute infection.

during establishment of latency in mouse sensory ganglia by wild-type herpes simplex type 1, viral DNA accumulates at levels exceeding those of the mutant virus by 2 to >3 orders of magnitude, whereas the levels of viral transcripts accumulate to similar levels in ganglia latently infected with wild-type virus and mutant virus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular biology of herpes simplex virus (HSV), the causative agent of herpes labialis, herpes genitalis, and herpes encephalitis.
the molecular biology of herpes simplex virus (HSV), a ubiquitous pathogen which is a major cause of genital disease in humans.
the molecular basis of the establishment of latency in the mouse trigeminal and dorsal root ganglia by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the thymidine kinase mutant virus is not able to produce infectious virions, but it can produce viral transcripts, and the transcripts are not degraded, but rather are maintained in the cell, which may be a mechanism of establishing latency.
the thymidine kinase-deficient virus is a replication-deficient virus and the wild-type is replication-proficient virus.
the establishment of latency by HSV is a complex and dynamic process that involves both viral and cellular factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
wild-type virus establishes latency in a two-stage process.
the accumulation of herpes simplex viral (HSV) transcripts and DNA is similar during the acute phase of infection of ganglia with either thymidine kinase (TK) negative mutants or wild-type virus.
, during the establishment of latent infection in mice, herpes simplex virus DNA accumulates in trigeminal ganglion neurons in a stepwise fashion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
thymidine kinase-defective mutants establish latent infections in mice but are severely impaired in acute ganglionic viral replication and productive cycle gene expression.

there is no clear distinction between acute ganglionic infections by wild-type and mutant viruses, but there is an abrupt change in viral nucleic acid accumulation and productive-cycle gene transcription in ganglia infected by wild-type virus that is coincident with the establishment of latent infection.
the establishment of HSV latency is a complex, multistep process, and the establishment of a latent infection does not necessarily mean that the infection is latent.
